text: It's 8:40 on a Monday morning. The service desk gets a call: the order management system throws errors every time a rep tries to apply a discount code at checkout. Three reps have reported it in ten minutes, and the supervisor says it's happening on roughly one in five transactions — customers are complaining, and reps can't work around it manually. You're the analyst taking this call, and it's the fourth time this exact symptom has shown up this month.

Your first move is incident management, and your first move there is triage, not investigation. You log it: service affected is checkout discounting, impact is roughly twenty percent of transactions with revenue and reputation at stake, and urgency is high since it's happening right now. That combination pushes it to high priority. Given the pattern from prior occurrences, you escalate straight to the engineer who already knows the fix. The engineer restarts the discount-pricing microservice, codes start working again, and the incident is resolved in minutes — with nobody yet knowing why it keeps failing.

A restart-and-move-on is reasonable for one incident. But a fourth identical occurrence in a month is exactly the pattern that should trigger problem identification — it isn't bad luck, it's a recurring cause incident management keeps papering over. A problem record opens, linked to all four incidents. Problem control digs into the logs and finds the microservice has a memory leak, crashing roughly every seven to ten days. Since a permanent fix isn't ready, this becomes a known error, with restarting the service recorded as the official workaround.

Engineering identifies the real fix: a corrected version of the service with the leak patched. This isn't a standard change — it's new code in a revenue-facing path — so it needs genuine assessment, making it a normal change. It goes through a defined evaluation covering what's changing, the rollback plan, and who signs off given the revenue at stake. Because the known error already has a working interim fix and nothing is down right now, there's no need to rush this as an emergency change — it's assessed, approved, and scheduled for a quiet deployment window.

The patched service deploys in its scheduled window, and engineering monitors it for two weeks with no further crashes and no recurrence. The known error closes, referencing the change that fixed it. The problem record closes, referencing that known error. The original incident, and the three before it, finally has a documented explanation and a permanent resolution instead of a fix that was turning into a monthly ritual.
